Vignette: Rohan, Age 29

Rohan grew up in a close-knit South Asian household where hard work and quiet resilience were the unspoken rules of family life. By his mid-twenties, he had built something he was genuinely proud of — a small but steady painting business, mostly residential work, the kind that kept his hands busy and let his mind wander in a way he found peaceful. He married his wife, Priya, two years ago, and life had a shape to it that felt right.

That shape changed on a Tuesday evening fourteen months ago. Rohan had finished a job in an unfamiliar part of the city and was walking back to his van, paint-spattered and tired, carrying his equipment bag over one shoulder. Two men approached him from behind. One pressed something hard into the small of his back — he still isn't certain whether it was a knife or a gun — and told him not to move. They took his phone, his wallet, his van keys, and the bag with his brushes and rollers. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. When it was over, Rohan stood alone on the pavement, unable to move for several minutes, certain that he was about to die even though the men were already gone.

He filed a police report that night but told Priya only that he'd been robbed, keeping his voice flat and practical. He replaced his equipment within a week. He went back to work. From the outside, it looked like he had handled it.

Inside, something had not returned to its original position. Rohan finds himself replaying the moment constantly — not as a memory he chooses to revisit, but as something that arrives without permission. He will be rolling paint along a ceiling, a task that once emptied his mind in a satisfying way, and suddenly he is back on that pavement, heart slamming, certain the pressure at his back is returning. He has to stop and grip the ladder until the feeling passes. Some days it does not pass quickly.

He no longer parks his van in side streets. He will circle a block for twenty minutes to find a spot on a main road with foot traffic, even when it costs him time he doesn't have. He avoids evening jobs entirely now, turning down work that would require him to finish after dark, telling clients his schedule is full. Priya has noticed that he takes a longer route home, one that adds fifteen minutes to the drive. When she asks about it, he changes the subject.

Sleep is its own problem. He lies awake cataloguing sounds — a door in the hallway, a car slowing outside — and when he does sleep, he wakes from dreams he can't always remember but that leave him with a residue of dread that sits with him through breakfast. He is exhausted in a way that rest doesn't touch.

Priya has tried to reach him. She is patient and perceptive, and she knows something is wrong in a way that goes beyond what he has told her. But Rohan comes from a family where men managed things internally, and there is a part of him that experiences his own distress as a kind of weakness he has not yet found a way to accept. He worries that if he speaks it aloud, it will become more real. He also worries, quietly and persistently, that he is simply not the same person he was before that evening — that the man who used to find genuine pleasure in the smell of fresh paint and the clean lines of a finished wall is somehow less available to him now.

He still goes to work every day. He is still good at what he does. But he moves through his days with a vigilance that never fully switches off, scanning faces, tracking exits, bracing — always bracing — for something he cannot name but cannot stop expecting.
